name: Aoki Lock
keyCorrections: If they pull their leg free, your figure-four was too shallow — re-lock higher on the thigh.
If you can't finish, your hip angle is wrong — rotate your hips toward them, not away.
If they stack you, release the grip and reset — don't fight the stack.
description: A kneebar from 50/50 or leg entanglement that uses a special figure-four grip and hip rotation to finish quickly without requiring full saddle control.
shortInstruction: Figure-four grip on the leg, rotate your hips toward their hip, extend the leg — the Aoki lock is a fast kneebar from 50/50.
summary: The Aoki lock (named after Shinya Aoki) is a kneebar variation from 50/50 guard that uses a unique grip: instead of controlling the leg with both hands in standard kneebar fashion, you lock a figure-four grip around their thigh. This grip gives you exceptional control of their hip rotation while your hip movement applies the hyper-extension on their knee. The Aoki lock is effective because it finishes quickly and doesn't require the full saddle or ashi garami position.
whyItWorks: The figure-four grip around their thigh prevents them from rotating their hip out of the kneebar.
It finishes from 50/50, a position where heel hooks are the primary threat — the Aoki lock catches opponents focused on heel defense.
The finish comes from hip rotation rather than pulling the leg — making it mechanically efficient.
Danaher principle: control the hip to control the knee — the figure-four grip is hip control.
commonMistakes: Not locking the figure-four grip deep enough on the thigh — a shallow grip lets them slip out.
Pulling the leg straight back instead of rotating the hips — the Aoki lock is a rotational kneebar.
Letting the opponent sit back and pull their heel free — maintain forward pressure.
Releasing the grip when they start to escape — the figure-four must stay tight throughout.
coachingCues: Figure-four deep on the thigh, not the calf.
Rotate your hips, don't pull the leg.
50/50 to Aoki lock — one movement, no pause.
Feel the hip rotation — that's the finish mechanism.
safetySummary: The Aoki lock hyper-extends the knee — apply pressure slowly and respect the tap.
Be aware that the figure-four grip can also put pressure on your own knee if you twist too aggressively.
Not recommended for beginners — requires kneebar mechanics understanding.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: 50/50 or leg entanglement: figure-four grip on their thigh → rotate hips toward their hip → extend their leg → finish.

decisionTree.action: The Aoki lock works as a chain from the heel hook threat: bait the heel defense, switch to Aoki.

decisionTree.condition: they defend the Aoki by turning their hip

moneyDetails: Lock the figure-four high on their thigh — as close to their hip as possible for maximum control.
Your grip should be: one hand grabs your own wrist, the other grabs their ankle — this creates the figure-four.
Rotate your hips toward their hip, not toward their foot — hip rotation creates the hyper-extension.
Keep their foot pinned to your hip as you rotate — this prevents them from kicking free.
nextStep: After the Aoki lock, learn the standard kneebar and the heel hook from 50/50.
fixItFast: Figure-four keeps slipping? Lock it higher on the thigh, closer to the hip.
Can't finish? Your hips aren't rotating enough — focus on bringing your hip toward their hip.
They sit back? Drive forward into them — don't let them create distance.
